robotics-controls-01-forward-kinematics-.essentialQuestion: Where does a two-joint planar arm tip land for known link lengths and joint angles?
robotics-controls-01-forward-kinematics-.verifiedBoundary: For two ideal rigid revolute links, x=L1 cos(theta1)+L2 cos(theta1+theta2) and y=L1 sin(theta1)+L2 sin(theta1+theta2); theta2 is relative to link 1.
robotics-controls-01-forward-kinematics-.analogy: Engineering intuition: model the planar 2r forward kinematics as a *specific mathematical contract*, not a generic robot behavior; verify each assumption before transferring the method to a physical system.

starter.plainStart: For two ideal rigid revolute links, x=L1 cos(theta1)+L2 cos(theta1+theta2) and y=L1 sin(theta1)+L2 sin(theta1+theta2); theta2 is relative to link 1.
starter.tryThis: Implement fk(L1,L2,t1,t2) with Math.cos/Math.sin; compare (0.4,0.3) within 1e-9 m.
starter.helper: Work strictly in the synthetic coordinate system and units defined below. Check the worked numerical model before attempting variations.

technical.scope: Synthetic, offline educational case. Rigid planar links, zero joint offsets, exact angles; not a physical collision or calibration model. Reference: https://modernrobotics.northwestern.edu/nu-gm-book-resource/inverse-kinematics-of-open-chains/

reasoningSteps: Model: L1=0.40 m, L2=0.30 m; base at (0,0); theta1=0 rad and relative theta2=+pi/2 rad, positive counterclockwise.
Resolve link vectors: first link (0.40,0.00) m; second link (0.00,0.30) m because its absolute heading is theta1+theta2.
Sum vectors: x=0.400000 m, y=0.300000 m; Euclidean reach sqrt(x^2+y^2)=0.500000 m, within [|L1-L2|,L1+L2]=[0.10,0.70] m.
Independent inverse check: subtract the first-link endpoint (0.40,0.00) m from the tip to recover the second vector (0,0.30) m and its 90 degree heading.
Falsifiable claim: treating theta2 as an absolute world angle works for theta1=0 but fails at theta1=pi/2, theta2=pi/2, where the correct tip is (-0.30,+0.40) m, not (+0.00,+0.70) m.

Controlled lab: change theta1 to pi/2 and recompute with relative theta1+theta2; explicit planar 2R derivation and Jacobian from Introduction to Open-Source Robotics: https://www.osrobotics.org/osr/kinematics/forward_kinematics.html

Sweep theta1 over {0,pi/2,pi} with theta2=pi/2: assert a 0.50 m tip radius in every case; explain why a reach-only test cannot establish collisions or joint limits.

robotics-controls-02-inverse-kinematics-.essentialQuestion: Can a reachable tip target have more than one valid elbow configuration?
robotics-controls-02-inverse-kinematics-.verifiedBoundary: For planar 2R: cos(theta2)=(x²+y²-L1²-L2²)/(2L1L2); each admissible sign of sin(theta2) defines a branch, except coincident branches at boundaries.
robotics-controls-02-inverse-kinematics-.analogy: Engineering intuition: model the 2r inverse solutions and reachability as a *specific mathematical contract*, not a generic robot behavior; verify each assumption before transferring the method to a physical system.

starter.plainStart: For planar 2R: cos(theta2)=(x²+y²-L1²-L2²)/(2L1L2); each admissible sign of sin(theta2) defines a branch, except coincident branches at boundaries.

robotics-controls-03-jacobian-singularit.essentialQuestion: How does a joint-velocity request map to end-effector velocity, and when does this mapping lose rank?
robotics-controls-03-jacobian-singularit.verifiedBoundary: The planar 2R Jacobian is the derivative of position with respect to joint angles; det J=L1L2 sin(theta2) for the standard coordinate convention.
robotics-controls-03-jacobian-singularit.analogy: Engineering intuition: model the 2r velocity jacobian and singularity as a *specific mathematical contract*, not a generic robot behavior; verify each assumption before transferring the method to a physical system.

starter.plainStart: The planar 2R Jacobian is the derivative of position with respect to joint angles; det J=L1L2 sin(theta2) for the standard coordinate convention.

reasoningSteps: Multiply by joint-rate vector (0.20,0.10) rad/s: tip velocity v=(-0.090,+0.080) m/s.
Independent cross-check: finite-difference the forward kinematics with h=1e-6 s and joint angles advanced by rate*h; recovered velocity matches within about 1e-6 m/s.
det J=(-0.30)(0)-(-0.30)(0.40)=+0.120 m²/rad²; rank is two at this posture.

At theta1=0 and theta2=0 rad, det J=0 and instantaneous horizontal tip velocity is impossible. Near this posture, theta2=0.01 rad and desired tip velocity (+0.010,0.000) m/s require joint rates (qdot1,qdot2)=(+2.49991667,-5.83330556) rad/s; at theta2=0.001 rad, the rates grow to (+24.99999167,-58.33333056) rad/s. These are mathematical inverse-velocity demands, not safe actuator commands; no inverse can recover the missing direction at exact singularity.
Falsifiable statement: a 2R arm always has two independent Cartesian velocity directions is false at theta2=0. Source: https://modernrobotics.northwestern.edu/nu-gm-book-resource/5-3-singularities/

robotics-controls-04-frame-transform-inv.essentialQuestion: How can a robot-local sensor reading be placed in a world frame without confusing the transform direction?
robotics-controls-04-frame-transform-inv.verifiedBoundary: For a planar rigid transform, p_world=R(theta_world_base) p_base+t_world_base and p_base=R^T(p_world-t).
robotics-controls-04-frame-transform-inv.analogy: Engineering intuition: model the coordinate-frame composition and inversion as a *specific mathematical contract*, not a generic robot behavior; verify each assumption before transferring the method to a physical system.

reasoningSteps: Define robot base origin at (1.00,2.00) m in world coordinates and world-from-base yaw +90°; a synthetic sensor position is (0.20,0.10) m in base coordinates.

Counterexample: translating before rotation yields R( [1.20,2.10] )=(-2.10,1.20) m, not the world point; matrix multiplication order is not interchangeable.
Variation: with yaw 0°, point becomes (1.20,2.10) m; changing the reference frame changes coordinates, not the physical point.

robotics-controls-05-differential-wheel-.essentialQuestion: What left/right wheel speeds yield a desired center velocity and yaw rate?
robotics-controls-05-differential-wheel-.verifiedBoundary: For wheel-track width b, v_left=v-omega*b/2 and v_right=v+omega*b/2; inverse v=(left+right)/2, omega=(right-left)/b.
robotics-controls-05-differential-wheel-.analogy: Engineering intuition: model the differential-drive chassis and wheel speeds as a *specific mathematical contract*, not a generic robot behavior; verify each assumption before transferring the method to a physical system.

Counterexample: doubling track width to 1.00 m while retaining the same wheel speeds halves omega to 0.20 rad/s; robot geometry cannot be ignored.
With both wheels 0.60 m/s, omega=0 rad/s and ideal instantaneous turning radius is unbounded (straight motion).

The model constrains lateral body-frame speed to zero; wheel slip/unequal radii violate it. Source: https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/kinematics-and-odometry/differential-drive-kinematics.html

robotics-controls-06-differential-drive-.essentialQuestion: How do unequal wheel increments advance a differential drive in a curved segment?
robotics-controls-06-differential-drive-.verifiedBoundary: For constant incremental curvature and dtheta≠0, ds=(dR+dL)/2, dtheta=(dR-dL)/b, R=ds/dtheta, dx=R sin(dtheta), dy=R(1-cos(dtheta)) in the initial body frame.
robotics-controls-06-differential-drive-.analogy: Engineering intuition: model the exact constant-curvature wheel odometry as a *specific mathematical contract*, not a generic robot behavior; verify each assumption before transferring the method to a physical system.

starter.plainStart: For constant incremental curvature and dtheta≠0, ds=(dR+dL)/2, dtheta=(dR-dL)/b, R=ds/dtheta, dx=R sin(dtheta), dy=R(1-cos(dtheta)) in the initial body frame.
starter.tryThis: Integrate the wheel increments with the exact sine/cosine arc formulas.
starter.helper: Work strictly in the synthetic coordinate system and units defined below. Check the worked numerical model before attempting variations.

technical.scope: Synthetic, offline educational case. Pose may drift unbounded over multiple steps with slip/bias; exact for chosen ideal constant-curvature segment. Reference: https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/kinematics-and-odometry/differential-drive-kinematics.html
technical.versionCaution: Check the cited canonical reference for platform/API changes; this lesson is not validated for live robot actuation.

reasoningSteps: Assume no slip, wheel increments dL=0.20 m and dR=0.30 m, track width b=0.50 m and initial pose (x,y,yaw)=(0,0,0).
Compute center arc length ds=(0.20+0.30)/2=0.25 m and heading change dtheta=(0.30-0.20)/0.50=+0.20 rad.
Turn radius R=ds/dtheta=1.25 m; exact arc integration gives dx=0.248336663 m, dy=0.024916778 m, heading=+0.20 rad.
Independent geometry check: chord distance sqrt(dx²+dy²)=2*R*sin(dtheta/2)=0.249583542 m, slightly shorter than arc length 0.25 m.

Counterexample: naive straight projection dx=ds=0.25,dy=0 misplaces the robot in a turn; midpoint projection is also only approximate. A numerical counterexample occurs at ds=0.25 m, dtheta=1e-9 rad: in IEEE-754 binary64 arithmetic, 1-cos(dtheta) rounds to zero and the direct radius-based formula falsely returns dy=0, although the true lateral increment is approximately +1.25e-10 m.

For robust exact integration use half-angle coordinates dx=ds*sinc(dtheta/2)*cos(dtheta/2), dy=ds*sinc(dtheta/2)*sin(dtheta/2), where sinc(z)=sin(z)/z and sinc(0)=1. Derive this by integrating the fixed-curvature chassis twist; it avoids subtraction cancellation and has the continuous limit dx=ds, dy=0 at dtheta=0. Negative yaw reverses the sign of dy; pure in-place rotation ds=0 changes yaw without translation. The no-slip, constant-curvature model is an odometry estimate, not ground truth; Modern Robotics 13.4: https://modernrobotics.northwestern.edu/nu-gm-book-resource/13-4-odometry/

robotics-controls-07-wheel-encoder-quant.essentialQuestion: How does digital encoder resolution limit inferred wheel travel?
robotics-controls-07-wheel-encoder-quant.verifiedBoundary: If N signed counts represent one wheel revolution at the wheel shaft, travel=counts*(2*pi*r/N); quantization step=2*pi*r/N.
robotics-controls-07-wheel-encoder-quant.analogy: Engineering intuition: model the encoder counts, resolution, and distance as a *specific mathematical contract*, not a generic robot behavior; verify each assumption before transferring the method to a physical system.

starter.plainStart: If N signed counts represent one wheel revolution at the wheel shaft, travel=counts*(2*pi*r/N); quantization step=2*pi*r/N.

technical.scope: Synthetic, offline educational case. Assumes wheel-shaft count definition, fixed effective rolling radius and zero slip. Reference: https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/kinematics-and-odometry/differential-drive-kinematics.html
technical.versionCaution: Check the cited canonical reference for platform/API changes; this lesson is not validated for live robot actuation.

reasoningSteps: Let wheel radius r=0.050 m and wheel-shaft encoder resolution N=2048 counted transitions per revolution (after any quadrature and gear-ratio interpretation).
One count represents 2*pi*0.05/2048=0.0001533980788 m; 1024 positive counts represent 0.157079633 m along the rolling direction.
Independent angular check: 1024/2048 revolution is 0.5 rev or pi radians; arc distance r*pi=0.157079633 m.
With 2048 counts the inferred travel is 0.314159265 m; using 1024 ticks per rev by mistake doubles the answer.
For rounding to nearest count, a single reading has ideal displacement quantization uncertainty no larger than half a count, about 0.0000766990 m, excluding systematic wheel errors.

Counterexample: encoder counts alone do not establish wheel-ground travel if the wheel slips or the count resolution is measured at a motor before gearing. Source background: https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/kinematics-and-odometry/differential-drive-kinematics.html

reasoningSteps: Define dimensionless state x, setpoint r=1, sample time dt=0.10 s, simulated integrator plant x[k+1]=x[k]+0.1*u[k] and gain Kp=4 s^-1, no saturation.

robotics-controls-10-integrator-antiwind.essentialQuestion: What happens to a PI controller's integral term when the actuator saturates for repeated positive error?
robotics-controls-10-integrator-antiwind.verifiedBoundary: One anti-windup scheme freezes integrator updates when the candidate command is saturated and error would drive it further into saturation.
robotics-controls-10-integrator-antiwind.analogy: Engineering intuition: model the conditional integration under output saturation as a *specific mathematical contract*, not a generic robot behavior; verify each assumption before transferring the method to a physical system.

starter.plainStart: One anti-windup scheme freezes integrator updates when the candidate command is saturated and error would drive it further into saturation.
starter.tryThis: Simulate ten fixed-error steps with and without conditional integration.
starter.helper: Work strictly in the synthetic coordinate system and units defined below. Check the worked numerical model before attempting variations.

technical.scope: Synthetic, offline educational case. Synthetic fixed-error study, not closed-loop transient tuning; policy must be checked for sign, limits and reset behavior. Reference: https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/advanced-controls/controllers/pidcontroller.html
technical.versionCaution: Check the cited canonical reference for platform/API changes; this lesson is not validated for live robot actuation.

reasoningSteps: Use a discrete synthetic PI controller with proportional gain Kp=2, integral gain Ki=1 s^-1, fixed positive error e=2, dt=0.1 s, and actuator output restricted to [-1,+1].
Initial integral I0=0; proportional contribution Kp*e=4 already exceeds +1, so the applied command clips to +1.
Naive integration updates I[k+1]=I[k]+e*dt; after 10 identical errors I10=2, and computed raw command is 4+1*2=6, while actuator still applies only +1.
Conditional anti-windup freezes I=0 for each step when the raw output is above +1 and the positive error would increase saturation; raw output stays 4, applied +1.
Independent check: summation of ten error rectangles gives 10*(2)*(0.1)=2; bounded integral remains 0 under the stated policy.

Counterexample with stored I=2: at subsequent error e=-0.25, raw output is 2*(-0.25)+1*2=+1.50 and clips +1, whereas conditional I=0 gives raw -0.50; output saturation alone does not erase the accumulated integral state. Context: https://docs.wpilib.org/en/latest/docs/software/advanced-controls/controllers/pidcontroller.html

labPlan: Simulate ten fixed-error samples with Kp=2, Ki=1 s^-1, e=2, dt=0.10 s and output limit +/-1, using both naive and saturation-aware conditional integrators.
Assert naive integral I10=2 and raw command 6, while conditional integration retains I10=0 and raw command 4; both applied commands clip to +1.

Now set a one-step test error e=-0.25 without first updating I: assert naive raw command +1.50 (still clips positive) versus guarded raw command -0.50 (negative), exposing wrong-direction windup recovery.

robotics-controls-11-scalar-kalman-updat.essentialQuestion: How does sensor uncertainty determine the weight of a new positional observation?
robotics-controls-11-scalar-kalman-updat.verifiedBoundary: For independent Gaussian scalar prior P and measurement variance R, K=P/(P+R), x_post=x_prior+K(z-x_prior), P_post=(1-K)P.
robotics-controls-11-scalar-kalman-updat.analogy: Engineering intuition: model the scalar measurement fusion and variance as a *specific mathematical contract*, not a generic robot behavior; verify each assumption before transferring the method to a physical system.

starter.plainStart: For independent Gaussian scalar prior P and measurement variance R, K=P/(P+R), x_post=x_prior+K(z-x_prior), P_post=(1-K)P.
starter.tryThis: Compute gain, mean and posterior variance with independent precision-weighted equation.
starter.helper: Work strictly in the synthetic coordinate system and units defined below. Check the worked numerical model before attempting variations.

technical.scope: Synthetic, offline educational case. Single scalar linear Gaussian independent measurement update; no prediction step, correlated noise or outlier rejection. Reference: https://docs.wpilib.org/en/latest/docs/software/advanced-controls/state-space/state-space-observers.html
technical.versionCaution: Check the cited canonical reference for platform/API changes; this lesson is not validated for live robot actuation.

reasoningSteps: Assume a prior location estimate x_prior=2.00 m with variance P=0.25 m² and independent unbiased sensor z=2.60 m with variance R=0.09 m².
Kalman gain K=0.25/(0.25+0.09)=0.735294118 (dimensionless).
Independent precision-weighted mean: (x_prior/P+z/R)/(1/P+1/R)=(2/.25+2.6/.09)/(4+11.111111)=2.441176471 m.
Counterexample: assigning both readings equal weight yields 2.30 m and disregards known unequal variances.

Variation: increase sensor variance to R=0.36 m²; gain decreases to 0.409836066 and updated mean becomes 2.245901639 m, so measurement is trusted less. Source: https://docs.wpilib.org/en/latest/docs/software/advanced-controls/state-space/state-space-observers.html

robotics-controls-12-trapezoid-profile.essentialQuestion: When does a symmetric speed-limited trajectory reach its specified maximum velocity?
robotics-controls-12-trapezoid-profile.verifiedBoundary: With rest-to-rest constant acceleration magnitude a and speed limit v_max, each acceleration ramp covers d_ramp=v_max²/(2a). If distance D<v_max²/a, use a triangular profile with peak sqrt(Da).
robotics-controls-12-trapezoid-profile.analogy: Engineering intuition: model the rest-to-rest trapezoidal versus triangular trajectories as a *specific mathematical contract*, not a generic robot behavior; verify each assumption before transferring the method to a physical system.

starter.plainStart: With rest-to-rest constant acceleration magnitude a and speed limit v_max, each acceleration ramp covers d_ramp=v_max²/(2a). If distance D<v_max²/a, use a triangular profile with peak sqrt(Da).

technical.scope: Synthetic, offline educational case. Ideal 1D symmetric motion, no jerk limits, obstacles, tracking error, or hardware safety claims. Reference: https://docs.wpilib.org/en/latest/docs/software/advanced-controls/controllers/trapezoidal-profiles.html
technical.versionCaution: Check the cited canonical reference for platform/API changes; this lesson is not validated for live robot actuation.

reasoningSteps: Assume an ideal one-dimensional robot translation D=2.00 m, rest-to-rest, maximum acceleration a=1.00 m/s² and speed limit v_max=1.00 m/s.
Acceleration duration t_acc=v_max/a=1.00 s; acceleration distance=0.5*a*t_acc²=0.50 m; deceleration repeats 0.50 m.
Remaining constant-speed distance is 2.00-1.00=1.00 m, so cruise lasts 1.00 s and total time is 3.00 s.
Independent area-under-speed check: triangular ramp areas 0.5+0.5 m and cruise rectangle 1.0 m sum to 2.00 m.
Counterexample: for distance D=0.40 m, there is insufficient room to reach 1.00 m/s; peak is sqrt(0.40*1)=0.632455532 m/s and total time is 2sqrt(0.40/1)=1.264911064 s.

Changing a or v_max can change the regime; neither trajectory establishes safety in a physical environment. Source: https://docs.wpilib.org/en/latest/docs/software/advanced-controls/controllers/trapezoidal-profiles.html
